question: Why is a single global AppContext (user + theme + notifications in one object) an anti-pattern?

options.text: Because context objects cannot be typed in TypeScript
options.explanation: TypeScript can type context objects just fine. That is not the cause of the problem.

options.text: Because changing any field causes all context subscribers to re-render
options.explanation: React cannot track which specific context fields a component uses. When notifications change, components that only read user also re-render.

options.text: Because a Provider with multiple fields cannot be memoized
options.explanation: useMemo works with objects of any structure. Memoization is possible, but it does not solve the problem — changing any field recreates the entire object.

options.text: Because createContext does not support objects with multiple fields
options.explanation: createContext perfectly well supports objects with any number of fields. The problem is not in syntax, but in behavior.

question: What does createStrictContext do compared to regular createContext?

options.text: This approach is outdated and no longer used
options.explanation: This approach is actively used in modern systems.

options.text: Returns a typed tuple [Context, useHook]
options.explanation: as const in the return value preserves the tuple type, allowing destructuring with correct types.

options.text: Automatically memoizes the context value
options.explanation: createStrictContext creates a context and hook, but value memoization must be done manually in the provider via useMemo.

options.text: Sets displayName for display in React DevTools
options.explanation: Context.displayName allows seeing 'ThemeContext.Provider' instead of 'Context.Provider' in DevTools.

options.text: Throws an error when the hook is used outside a provider
options.explanation: This is the main difference: the strict hook checks value !== undefined and throws an Error with a clear message.

question: Why must ComposeProviders use reduceRight instead of reduce?

options.text: So that the first provider in the array becomes the outermost in the tree
options.explanation: reduceRight starts from the end of the array and wraps each next one on the outside. The first element of the array becomes the outermost provider.

options.text: reduceRight is faster for arrays of providers
options.explanation: Performance is not the difference here — provider arrays are small. The reason is nesting order.

options.text: Because reduce does not work with JSX elements
options.explanation: reduce works fine with JSX. The only difference is order — with reduce the first in the array becomes the innermost.

options.text: So that children always end up in the correct position
options.explanation: children are always passed as the initial accumulator value — this does not depend on choosing reduce/reduceRight.

question: You are writing a NotificationBell component that shows the notification count. The application uses separated contexts: UserContext, ThemeContext, NotificationsContext. Under which action should NotificationBell re-render?

options.text: The user switched the theme from light to dark
options.explanation: NotificationBell is subscribed only to NotificationsContext. A theme change in ThemeContext will not cause it to re-render.

options.text: The user logged out
options.explanation: Logging out updates UserContext. NotificationBell is not subscribed to UserContext and will not re-render.

options.text: The user dismissed a notification
options.explanation: Dismissing a notification updates NotificationsContext — NotificationBell re-renders to show the updated count.

options.text: A new notification arrives
options.explanation: A new notification updates NotificationsContext, which NotificationBell is subscribed to.

question: Why use useRef instead of useState for a component's render counter?

options.text: Because ref can only be used for DOM elements
options.explanation: This is a common misconception. useRef can store any values, not just DOM references.

options.text: Because ref value persists between renders, but state does not
options.explanation: State also persists between renders — that is exactly what it is for. This is not a difference.

options.text: Because updating ref does not trigger a re-render, so the counter does not distort the measurement
options.explanation: If you use useState for the counter, each change would trigger an extra re-render, distorting the metric itself. useRef updates without re-render.

options.text: useRef is faster than useState
options.explanation: Speed is not the main point here. The fundamental reason is: ref updates do not cause re-renders.

question: How to correctly prevent unnecessary subscriber re-renders when using a Context Provider?

options.text: Use useCallback instead of useMemo for the context value
options.explanation: useCallback memoizes functions. For the context value object you need useMemo.

options.text: Wrap the Provider in React.memo
options.explanation: React.memo prevents the component from re-rendering due to unchanged props, but does not affect context subscriber re-renders.

options.text: Pass primitives in value instead of objects
options.explanation: Primitives help for individual fields, but the full context is usually an object. The correct solution is useMemo to stabilize the object.

options.text: Memoize the context value via useMemo
options.explanation: useMemo stabilizes the reference to the value object. If dependencies have not changed, Context.Provider receives the same object and does not trigger subscriber re-renders.

question: A team is building a dashboard with real-time data: currency rates update every second, user data — on login. How should contexts be organized?

options.text: One context for all data — easier to manage
options.explanation: When currency rates update every second, all components including user interface will re-render. This leads to noticeable lag.

options.text: Use one context but wrap all components in React.memo
options.explanation: React.memo will not help: it prevents re-renders from props, but not from context changes. Context subscribers always re-render on context change.

options.text: Separate contexts: UserContext (rare) and CurrencyContext (frequent)
options.explanation: Data with different update frequencies should be in different contexts. Components showing the user name will not re-render on every currency update.

options.text: Context API is unsuitable for frequently updated data — Redux is needed
options.explanation: Context API is perfectly fine. The key is to separate data by frequency. For very high-frequency data (>10 times/sec) alternatives are worth considering, but once per second — context handles it.

question: What happens if you don't specify Context.displayName when creating a context?

options.text: In React DevTools the provider will show as 'Context.Provider' instead of 'ThemeContext.Provider'
options.explanation: displayName is only for debugging. In DevTools all contexts without displayName look the same — 'Context.Provider', making the component tree harder to read.

options.text: Context subscribers will not receive updates
options.explanation: displayName is purely a debugging property. The subscription and update mechanism does not depend on it.

options.text: The application will throw a compilation error
options.explanation: displayName is optional. Its absence does not affect application behavior.

options.text: useContext will not be able to find the correct provider
options.explanation: useContext identifies the provider by the Context object reference, not by name. displayName does not affect functionality.

question: Which of the following are correct uses of Context API?

options.text: Store a form state with 20 fields
options.explanation: Form state is local and not needed by other components. useState/useReducer in the form component is the right choice.

options.text: Store authenticated user data
options.explanation: The current user is needed in the header, sidebar, profile — this is global data, an ideal candidate for UserContext.

options.text: Store a product catalog list for pagination
options.explanation: Product list is server data specific to a particular page. React Query, SWR, or page-local state is better for this.

options.text: Store the active application theme (light/dark)
options.explanation: Theme is a classic use case for Context: global data, changes infrequently, needed in many components.

question: A developer created ThemeContext without createStrictContext, with defaultValue = null. The ThemeToggle component was forgotten to be wrapped in ThemeProvider. What will happen?

options.text: TypeScript will prevent compilation — null type does not match ThemeValue
options.explanation: TypeScript checks types, but if createContext<ThemeValue | null>(null) — this is a valid type. TS will not prevent the error if the developer intentionally included null in the type.

options.text: ThemeToggle will work with defaultValue = null without error — a silent bug
options.explanation: Without a strict hook, useContext will return defaultValue (null). The component may partially render without a visible error. The bug will be hard to detect — this is exactly what makes createStrictContext necessary.

options.text: React will automatically find the nearest ThemeProvider up the tree
options.explanation: React searches for a provider up the tree. If none found — returns defaultValue. There is no automatic protection.

options.text: The browser will throw a TypeError when accessing properties of null
options.explanation: It might, but only if the component tries to access a property of null (e.g. null.mode). This may happen, but the error will be unclear.
